catalog_migration.reason: Fully regenerate the published Great Crested Flycatcher plate to keep the complete title, taxonomy, measurements, specimen, supporting studies, ruler, and all five palette labels inside safe portrait and display margins. The corrected plate preserves the species identity and field-journal presentation while replacing the clipped composition; all visible content was independently re-reviewed.

profile.behavior: Usually forages from high perches, making short sallies after insects and returning to a perch; spends little time on the ground.
field_marks: Large, lean flycatcher with a broad-shouldered look, large head, and subtle peaked crest.
Brownish-gray head, throat, and breast contrast with a bright lemon-yellow belly.
Thick, straight dark bill, often with a paler base to the lower mandible.
Olive- to reddish-brown upperparts with pale-edged wing feathers.
Rufous-orange flashes in the wings and a long, rufous-brown tail.
Dark legs and feet; sexes alike in plumage.
profile.habitat: Open broadleaf or mixed woodlands, woodland edges, clearings, hedgerows, and other tree-rich habitats; typically uses the upper canopy and nests in cavities.

findings: The primary specimen is convincingly identifiable as a Great Crested Flycatcher: large-headed, lean proportions; subtly peaked crown; brownish-gray head and breast; lemon-yellow belly; reddish-brown upperparts; rufous wing and tail feathers; dark legs; and a thick, straight bill with a paler lower-mandible base all agree with the reference photographs and direct identification sources.

The primary specimen has one head, one beak, one visible eye, one tail, two plausibly attached legs with gripping feet, and a coherent pair of wings; the far-side wing is naturally occluded by the side-profile pose. No malformed, duplicated, or detached primary anatomy is visible.

The detached wing and bill/head studies are clearly labeled supplementary illustrations, remain visually separate from the primary specimen, and accurately reinforce the rufous flight-feather pattern, pale feather edging, peaked head, eye, and bill configuration.

Both depicted bills are complete from base to tip, straight and appropriately heavy at the base. Their mandibles are coherent and consistent with the clearest side-profile references; neither upper mandible appears truncated, reversed, or materially disproportionate.

All visible descriptive text was checked line by line. The common name, scientific name, family, habitat, behavior, six field-mark statements, measurements, study labels, and five palette labels are legible, correctly spelled, and reproduce the proposed facts without duplicated, omitted, substituted, or nonsensical wording.

Published measurements vary by source: All About Birds reports 17–21 cm, 27–40 g, and a 34 cm wingspan; Audubon reports 20–22 cm, 27–40 g, and 33–38 cm; Animal Diversity Web gives averages of 22.2 cm, 34 g, and 33 cm. The plate's 17–22 cm and 33–38 cm values form an inclusive synthesis of these direct measurements, and no two direct domains establish a single contrary range requiring a profile conflict.

The body-length diagram repeats the printed 17–22 cm (6.7–8.7 in) range, places 17 cm at the bottom and 22 cm at the top, increases in the correct direction, uses consistent units, contains no contradictory marker, and is explicitly labeled “SCHEMATIC — NOT TO SCALE.”
The plate contains no place name, ZIP code, coordinates, map, range depiction, or local-observation detail.
The composition is clear and well balanced: the primary specimen dominates appropriately, supporting studies are distinct, and the text and schematic remain readable without obscuring anatomy.
